payload.rationale: Observed: GISS LOTI Jan–Aug 2026 anomalies average ~1.22 C (sum 9.79), with August at 1.40, the highest so far. Beating 2025 (1.19) is nearly certain; the binding condition is the fixed contractual threshold of >1.28 C, which with two-decimal reporting effectively requires a reported annual of 1.29, i.e., Sep–Dec must average roughly 1.41 C or higher. Supporting evidence: NOAA CPC (10 Sep 2026) reports El Niño present and strengthening with >90% chance of a very strong event in fall/winter 2026–27, with eastern equatorial Pacific anomalies already exceeding +3.0 C. Transfer assumption: in prior developing strong El Niño years (e.g., 2023, 2015), GISS Sep–Dec anomalies ran well above the Jan–Aug mean and above the August value (2023: Aug 1.19 → Sep–Dec ~1.40 avg). Applying a similar late-year lift to a 2026 baseline already at 1.40 in August makes a Sep–Dec average of ≥1.41 more likely than not, though not assured because ENSO's global-temperature response lags by several months and may peak in early 2027. Too high risk: August's jump could partly be noise and be revised down; monthly noise (~0.1 C) over four months could leave the annual at 1.26–1.28, just short; the required Sep–Dec average equals the current single-month high. Too low risk: an El Niño this extreme, on top of the secular trend, could push Sep–Dec to 1.5+ C, comfortably clearing the threshold, and 2023's analogue suggests a rapid autumn surge. Net estimate ~0.65.
limitations: No fitted predictive distribution for Sep–Dec 2026 GISS anomalies; estimate relies on analogue reasoning from prior El Niño years.
GISS monthly values are subject to revision, which could move the Jan–Aug base either way.
Exact rounding/settlement handling of 'above 1.28' with two-decimal reporting is assumed to require a reported 1.29 or higher.
ENSO evidence is from a single CPC discussion; no seasonal global-temperature forecasts (e.g., GMSTA page contents) were supplied.
